summary:
Haiti does not criminalise same-sex conduct; the prohibition has been off the books since 1791. There is no legal mechanism for gender recognition, no statutory anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, and no hate-crime enhancement. The judiciary does not operate as a protection avenue in practice.

The legislature has twice moved to tighten the regime. In August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 Senate bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs, the good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. Both measures awaited a vote in the Chamber of Deputies as of November 2017.

Generalised state collapse drives the practical risk. Gangs control most of Port-au-Prince, the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented; no protection machinery functions. Outing in gang-controlled areas can be lethal for a visitor.

The US State Department's 2018 report recorded attitudes in Haiti as hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince. Human Rights Watch's 2018 world report found that LGBT persons in Haiti continued to face high levels of discrimination.

Visible advocacy carries a documented risk. Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, the national LGBTQ advocacy organisation, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince on 25 November 2019; press reports attributing the death to poisoning were never confirmed. ILGALAC, the regional LGBTI body, issued a mourning statement.

Trans people have additionally faced targeted harassment in the post-earthquake displacement camps, where they were identifiable to other residents and to camp authorities.
tangentialFactors:
De jure legality sits against a legislative trend in the opposite direction, so the statutory baseline understates exposure: a visitor reading only the criminal code would miss the pending advocacy and marriage penalties entirely.

Violence risk is not trans-specific in origin but is trans-specific in effect. Mob violence against perceived LGBT people, gang domination of the capital and the 2019 killing of a prominent activist show that visibility, not conduct, is the operative trigger.

Public-order offences remain a live channel of police contact. Trans visitors stay exposed to vagrancy-style fines and discretionary harassment, with no anti-discrimination law to constrain how a stop is handled.

Displacement settings concentrate the risk. Harassment documented in the post-earthquake camps indicates that crowded, poorly policed informal sites are among the least safe places for a visibly trans person.
localsOnly:
Haitian LGBT organisations operate under a proposed ban on public advocacy carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of roughly US$8,000, a threat that has shaped how Kouraj and comparable groups can work in public.

The Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs is a gatekeeping document for employment and university admission. Under the June 2017 Senate bill, a homosexuality finding could be used to refuse it, which converts institutional document checks into an exclusion mechanism for residents.

Residents have no route to legal gender recognition, so identity documents continue to display a sex marker that may not match presentation, and there is no anti-discrimination protection in employment, education or services to challenge the resulting treatment.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of both Senate bills after November 2017 is unresolved in the available sources; no source in the inventory records a Chamber of Deputies vote, withdrawal or enactment.

The cause of Charlot Jeudy's death is unresolved. Poisoning was reported but not confirmed, and no source in the inventory states an official finding or arrest.

Prison placement for trans detainees is not sourced. The inventory contains no rule on birth-sex versus identity housing, no trans-specific units, and no solitary or segregation practice, so nothing can be asserted about how Haiti houses trans prisoners.

The most recent official assessment of the hostility climate in the inventory dates from 2018, with a press account from 2019. Current official reporting on attitudes toward visibly trans visitors after that point is not sourced here.
